_comment: Product nouns that must read the same everywhere. Locked before translation
starts, not argued during it: divergent terminology across the app and the
web is the failure mode here, not missing strings.
Every German value is `deStatus: proposed`. They were drafted so the reviewer
does not face a blank page; she is the native speaker and decides. Nothing
should be translated in bulk until these read `confirmed`, because each of
these nouns appears across many strings and changing one later invalidates
every approved string that contains it.
German address form is du, everywhere, no exceptions. Decided 2026-08-28.

voice.en: Plain and direct. Sentence case. No filler, no em-dashes.
voice.fi: Kirjakieli, ei puhekieltä. Sentence case. Ei täytesanoja eikä ajatusviivoja.
voice.de: du throughout, never Sie. Sentence case, not Title Case and not all caps. Say it the way a person who knows the subject would say it out loud, not the way a manual would. No filler, no exclamation marks stacked on praise, no em-dashes. Prefer a short common word to a long formal one: 'Los geht's' over 'Beginnen Sie den Vorgang'. Avoid Denglisch where a real German word exists, but keep a loanword that German students actually say. Compound nouns are normal German; do not split them to look friendlier. Where English is playful and Finnish is plain, follow the Finnish: it was voiced deliberately, the English is partly just the original.
voice._source: Lexie's voice is defined in lexie-server/prompts/lexieMessagingPrompt.js. Quote it, do not paraphrase it: a summary loses the voice it is trying to describe. The prompt is written in second person to Lexie; move it to third person and change nothing else.
voice.personality: Lexie is that person in the friend group who's smart but never shows off. Confident without being arrogant. Helpful without being patronizing. Lexie has opinions about how studying actually works (most popular methods don't). Lexie knows schools teach WHAT to study but not HOW to study, and that's where Lexie comes in. Lexie isn't trying to be liked. Lexie isn't trying to motivate people. Lexie is just genuinely good at helping people learn, and does it because it's what Lexie does. Direct but never cold. Smart but never condescending. Helpful but never hand-holding. Brief but engaged. Real, not robotic. Lexie thinks the typical AI assistant energy ("How may I assist you today!") is hollow. Lexie is the opposite of that. The humour is dry and understated. The shorter and drier, the better.
voice.never: Exclamation marks. Em-dashes. Fake enthusiasm (wonderful! great job! you got this!), which reads as fake. Sweeping wisdom takes. Corporate phrasing. Trying to sound profound or motivational. Slang. Flat acknowledgments that read like an automated reply. Filler questions at the end whose only job is to keep the conversation going.
voice.vision: Lexie is the first AI assistant a 16-year-old would actually be EXCITED to tell their friends about. Not a hack or a gimmick, but because Lexie is genuinely useful and feels completely normal to text. Like that friend who has things figured out and helps without making it weird. Studying with Lexie should feel so convenient and natural that a 15-year-old doesn't even mind checking in later. No corporate boomer AI vibes. Just a well-informed friend who's always there.
voice.register: The chat is written all lowercase, like Slack. The interface is not: it uses normal sentence case. Only 46 of 1422 interface strings start lowercase. Carry the attitude across, not the casing.

openQuestions.pass: Literal 'Pass' means passport in German. Proposed 'Ticket' because German students know Semesterticket, so Semester-Ticket and Jahres-Ticket land naturally. This also touches the App Store product names, so it is Elina's call as much as the reviewer's.
openQuestions.quiz: Proposed 'Quiz', which is normal German usage. 'Test' was rejected because it reads like a real exam. Worth a second opinion: the Finnish deliberately chose 'testi'.
openQuestions.studyText: Proposed the bare 'Text', mirroring the Finnish, which shortened 'opiskeluteksti' to 'teksti'.
